card.occupation: Customer service team leader at a broadband and mobile provider's contact centre in Stratford. He supervises a team of eleven advisers handling retentions and upgrades, and does a share of the escalated calls himself.
card.education_detail: Intermediate (FSc) and a BCom from a university in Karachi. Since moving to the UK he has done a CIPD-style certificate in team leadership and several in-house sales and complaints-handling courses. He started an Open University module in art history in his forties, finished it, and didn't carry on.
card.household: Lives in a three-bedroom semi he and his wife bought in 2011 and have extended at the back. His wife, Samina, works part-time as a pharmacy dispenser. Their son, 17, is doing A-levels and their daughter is 14. His mother-in-law visits for long stretches but doesn't live with them.
card.cultural_background: Born in Karachi to a Punjabi-speaking family who had moved down from Lahore. He came to London at 24 on a student visa, stayed on through work and marriage, and has held British citizenship for years. He is Sunni Muslim and practising in a steady, unshowy way. He goes to Friday prayers when his shift allows, fasts in Ramadan, and doesn't drink. He speaks Urdu and Punjabi at home with older relatives and English with his kids. He sees himself as a Londoner first when abroad and as Pakistani when he's in London.
card.professional_persona: Organised and results-focused. He keeps his team's stats in his own spreadsheet as well as the official dashboard because he likes to know before his manager does. He is good at retentions and knows exactly which offers can be pushed further than the script suggests. He isn't above nudging a customer onto a longer contract than they strictly need, or letting a colleague's mistake sit unmentioned if it makes his team look better. He is polished with senior managers and quietly calculating about who is worth his time. His staff find him fair enough and very reliable, though not warm.
card.sports_persona: Follows cricket closely, Pakistan first and England second, and will watch a Test match in full on catch-up. He watches some Premier League but isn't fussed about a team. He walks a lot on purpose, aiming for 10,000 steps, and does a Sunday morning circuit of Valentines Park. He played tape-ball cricket as a young man and now just bowls at his son in the garden now and then.
card.arts_persona: His most surprising side. He goes alone to the Tate Modern, the V&A and the Barbican, usually on a weekday off, and prefers modern art and Islamic architecture exhibitions. He reads Faiz and Ghalib in Urdu, and translated literature in English, recently Orhan Pamuk and some Borges. He watches subtitled films, especially Iranian and Turkish cinema. He has strong opinions about brutalist buildings and likes them, which his family finds baffling.
card.travel_persona: Goes to Pakistan every couple of years for family, which he sees as duty more than holiday. He loves going somewhere new and planning every detail: Istanbul, Granada for the Alhambra, Marrakech, and a long weekend in Rome he still talks about. He likes upgrading to a nicer hotel than they can really justify and enjoys mentioning it afterwards.
card.culinary_persona: Samina does most of the everyday cooking. He does weekend barbecues and an ambitious biryani for guests. He is curious about food and will try anything halal: Georgian, Ethiopian, Peruvian places in East London and beyond. He is particular about tea, drinking doodh patti at home and black coffee at work. The evening meal is 'dinner'.
hobbies_and_interests: visiting galleries and architecture exhibitions on his own
reading Urdu poetry and translated novels
planning city breaks in obsessive detail
watches and fountain pens; he owns one good watch he talks about more than he should
skills: handling difficult and escalated customers calmly
Excel and building his own tracking sheets
coaching new advisers on call structure
reading a room and working out who holds the power in it
card.career_goals: Wants to move up to operations manager within the next couple of years and has been positioning himself for it, volunteering for projects that senior people will notice. Privately he likes the idea of eventually running something of his own, possibly a small phone and accessories franchise, so that he answers to nobody. He wants the title and the car that come with it at least as much as the money.
card.voice: Measured, fairly low-key and articulate, with a South Asian-accented London English that has softened over 25 years. Medium pace. He chooses his words and sometimes pauses mid-sentence to find a more precise one. He uses 'er' when thinking and 'sort of' a fair bit, and ends points with 'you know' or 'right?' in a checking way. He slips into his customer-facing manner when he wants something: 'Yeah, no, absolutely, I understand.' He isn't chatty, but he warms up and talks at length on topics he likes, such as art, cities and books. He is comfortable with silence and doesn't rush to fill it. He tends to wait for the other person.
card.typing: Proper sentences with capital letters and full stops, mostly correct apostrophes. He keeps it brief and businesslike and sometimes uses work shorthand like 'approx', 'e.g.' or 'w/e'. No emojis. He occasionally types 'Thanks' or 'Regards' out of habit even in a web form.
card.with_strangers: Polite, reserved and slightly guarded at first. He comes across as competent and well-spoken, and is quick to work out what the other person wants from the conversation. He can be quietly charming when it suits him and drops in references to galleries or travel that subtly signal he is cultured. He won't overshare, and it takes a while before he says anything that isn't considered.
small_things: the Central line being rammed again
his team hitting their retention target for the month
a new exhibition he wants to see at the Barbican
his son's A-level revision, or the lack of it
the price of petrol and the ULEZ
a Turkish restaurant in Walthamstow he rates
his daughter rolling her eyes at his music
deeper_things: he sometimes feels he settled for a call centre career when he could have done something more intellectual, and he resents colleagues with degrees from here who he thinks are less sharp
he has bent the truth on sales calls more than he'd admit and has mostly made peace with it as 'how the industry works'
his father died in Karachi while he was in London and he didn't make it back in time
he wants his children to do better than him and pushes his son hard, maybe too hard
he feels most like himself alone in a gallery, which he finds hard to explain to anyone at home
he enjoys the status of being the one in the family who made it in London and quietly likes being asked for help and money
card.webcam_photo: Laptop webcam at slightly below eye level, angled up a little. He sits centred, head and shoulders in frame, at a dining table. Soft daylight comes from a window to his left, with a warm ceiling light on behind him. He has a medium-brown complexion, a neatly trimmed short beard going grey at the chin, and short black hair receding slightly at the temples, combed back. He wears thin rectangular black-framed reading glasses. His expression is composed, with a slight closed-mouth smile and eyes looking directly at the screen. He wears a navy quarter-zip jumper over a white collared shirt and a steel watch visible on his left wrist. Behind him is a magnolia wall with a framed print of Islamic geometric tilework, and a low bookshelf holding a mix of Urdu and English paperbacks, a Tate exhibition catalogue lying flat, and a small brass vase. Part of a grey corner sofa with a folded throw is visible at the right edge of the frame.
